notes.one_line: A policy maker splits a budget over central and local protective resources and over candidate pickpocket locations while the thief picks a location (or opts out) by a multinomial logit whose utilities fall log-linearly in protective spending; the authors convexify the problem and derive closed-form optimal allocations for the base model (Theorem 2), with a fairness constraint of equal pickpocket probabilities (Theorem 3), and for a deterministic thief, where the fair allocation turns out optimal (Theorem 4). A Paris numerical study compares these allocations with two simple practitioner rules.
notes.question: How should a policy maker (e.g., the mayor of a city) allocate a limited financial budget R over local protective resources (per location, e.g., cameras, billboards, police officers), central protective resources (covering all locations, e.g., social-media awareness campaigns, the Boefproof app) and potential pickpocket locations, in order to minimize the overall pickpocket probability during a given period or event, when the thief's location choice follows a random utility (MNL) model with an opt-out option? Secondary questions: (i) what is the optimal allocation when every location must face the same pickpocket probability (fairness constraint)? (ii) what is the optimal allocation when the thief's decision process is deterministic with known preferences, as observed by the policy maker? (iii) how do these optimal allocations perform against simple intuitive rules used by policy makers (CLE, CELP), and how much extra budget is needed to keep the overall pickpocket probability stable during special events that make all locations more attractive?
notes.motivation_application: Organized crime in Europe: the latest Serious and Organized Crime Threat Assessment report estimates its annual impact on the EU economy at EUR 218 to 282 billion in GDP terms (cited as Luyten & Voronova, 2020); the Norwegian police estimated stolen goods at about EUR 2.3 million in 2018 for Oslo city center alone (Thorsen, 2018); more than 52 million pickpocketing attempts were reported in Europe in 2009 to 2015 (EUCPN, 2017a). Actions include the European Harmony project (Frans, 2010; led by Belgium with Europol, the Netherlands and the UK as partners), awareness campaigns (the Dutch Boefproof campaign, part of a larger campaign of the Dutch Ministry of Security and Justice using billboards, radio, social media and influencers; radio commercials in Prague, short videos in Brussels hotel rooms, warning templates sprayed on a pedestrian zone in Berlin) and traditional devices (camera surveillance, police patrols in metro stations and shopping halls). Fig. 1 (p. 581) shows billboards and a sprayed warning template. Policy makers must split a finite budget among such protective resources and among locations (metro stations, market squares, sightseeing spots). The paper's stated novelty is to include the thief's preferences over locations through an MNL model, following the discrete-choice approach to crime location choice in criminology (Bernasco & Nieuwbeerta, 2005; Kuralarasan & Bernasco, 2022), so that the causal link between the budget allocated and the location-specific pickpocket probability is captured. The application in Section 7 is the Paris 'pickpocket plan': Paris had over 40 million visitors in 2018 (Gadaud, 2019), and a June 2022 news bulletin (Bijlsma, 2022) revealed that the Paris police had reactivated the plan (more police at the Champs-Elysees, Montmartre, the Eiffel Tower, the Louvre and the Seine quays). Tourist attractions are the locations.
notes.model:
ACTORS. A policy maker and a thief. The thief may be a single person or an organized group of homogeneous individuals planning to pickpocket one location (fn. 3, p. 583). This is NOT a cooperative game: there are no coalitions and no characteristic function. Reader's characterization (the paper does not use the word Stackelberg for its own model): the policy maker commits to an allocation and the thief answers probabilistically with an MNL, a leader-follower structure. The paper links this to security games with quantal-response offenders (Section 2.1 and fn. 2, p. 582: the quantal response expression is the MNL expression, Jessie & Saari 2016).

SETS AND DATA (Section 3.1, p. 583). Potential pickpocket locations $N\subseteq\mathbb N$; local protective resources $L\subseteq\mathbb N$ (each protects one specific location); central protective resources $C\subseteq\mathbb N$ (protect all locations simultaneously); $N\cap(C\cup L)=\emptyset$, $L\cap C=\emptyset$, and $C,L\neq\emptyset$ (to avoid trivial cases). Maximal budget $R\in\mathbb R_{++}$.

DECISION. $x_{ij}\in\mathbb R_{++}$ is the budget for local resource type $j\in L$ at location $i\in N$; $x_k\in\mathbb R_{++}$ is the budget for central resource $k\in C$; $x=((x_{ij})_{i\in N,j\in L},(x_k)_{k\in C})$ is a budget allocation. Feasible set
$$\mathcal X=\Big\{x\in\mathbb R_{++}^{|N|\cdot|L|+|C|}\ \Big|\ \sum_{i\in N}\sum_{j\in L}x_{ij}+\sum_{k\in C}x_k\le R\Big\}.$$
The budget may be spent partially, and every resource type receives some strictly positive (possibly arbitrarily small) budget (p. 583). Reader's note: the open orthant is what makes the logarithms well defined (the paper invokes $x\in\mathbb R_{++}$ in the proof of Lemma 6).

THIEF (Section 3.2, pp. 583-584). Choice set $\mathcal C=N\cup\{0\}$, where $0$ is the opt-out (pickpocketing in another city or district, or staying home; fn. 4 says opt-outs are widespread and recommended, citing Campbell & Erdem 2019). Random utility $U_i(x)=V_i(x)+\varepsilon_i$ with $U_0(x)=V_0(x)=0$ (normalization, fn. 5) and i.i.d. type-I extreme value errors $\varepsilon_i\sim EV(0,1)$ (p. 584; fn. 7 justifies the choice). Deterministic utility, Eq. (2):
$$V_i(x)=\alpha_i-\sum_{j\in L}\beta_j\ln x_{ij}-\sum_{k\in C}\beta_k\ln x_k,\qquad \alpha_i\in\mathbb R_+,\ \beta_j,\beta_k\in\mathbb R_{++}.$$
$\alpha_i$ is an alternative-specific constant, the initial interest in location $i$ (e.g., tourists per time unit, distance to the thief's home, escape possibilities). $\beta$ is the thief's sensitivity to the risk perceived from a resource type; a local type has one $\beta_j$ for all locations. The thief is aware of the protection in place. The log-linear form gives diminishing marginal utility of protection (p. 584; fn. 6 says other concave forms are possible). MNL probabilities, Eq. (3):
$$\mathbb P_i(x)=\frac{\exp\{\alpha_i-\sum_{j\in L}\beta_j\ln x_{ij}-\sum_{k\in C}\beta_k\ln x_k\}}{1+\sum_{n\in N}\exp\{\alpha_n-\sum_{j\in L}\beta_j\ln x_{nj}-\sum_{k\in C}\beta_k\ln x_k\}},\qquad \mathbb P_0(x)=\frac{1}{1+\sum_{n\in N}\exp\{\cdots\}}.$$
The overall pickpocket probability is $\mathbb P(x)=\sum_{i\in N}\mathbb P_i(x)$.

POLICY MAKER'S PROBLEM. Eq. (1)/(4): $\mathscr P=\min_{x\in\mathcal X}\mathbb P(x)$. Eq. (4) as printed has $\sum_{k\in C}\beta_j\ln(x_j)$ in the numerator, a typo for $\beta_k\ln(x_k)$. $\mathbb P$ is not convex (fn. 10). By Observation 1, $\mathscr P$ is equivalent to $\max\mathbb P_0$, Eq. (5), and to
$$\mathscr B=\min_{x\in\mathcal X}\mathbb B(x),\qquad \mathbb B(x)=\sum_{i\in N}\exp\Big\{\alpha_i-\sum_{j\in L}\beta_j\ln x_{ij}-\sum_{k\in C}\beta_k\ln x_k\Big\}=\sum_{i\in N}\frac{e^{\alpha_i}}{\prod_{j\in L}x_{ij}^{\beta_j}\prod_{k\in C}x_k^{\beta_k}}$$
(product form = Lemma 6), with $\mathbb P=\mathbb B/(1+\mathbb B)$. The budget binds: $\sum_i\sum_j x_{ij}+\sum_k x_k=R$, Eq. (6), p. 585. Footnote 9 defines two problems as 'equivalent' if they share at least one optimal solution. Footnote 8: $\mathbb P\to0$ as $R\to\infty$ and $\mathbb P\to1$ as $R\to0$.

VARIANT 1: FAIRNESS (Section 5, Eq. (9), p. 585). $\overline{\mathcal X}=\{x\in\mathcal X:\mathbb P_i(x)=\mathbb P_{i'}(x)\ \forall i,i'\in N\}$, $\overline{\mathscr P}=\min_{x\in\overline{\mathcal X}}\mathbb P(x)$, equivalent to $\overline{\mathscr B}=\min_{x\in\overline{\mathcal X}}\mathbb B(x)$ (Observation 2). The constraint is non-linear, so Theorem 1 does not apply; a nested two-step procedure with induction is used.

VARIANT 2: DETERMINISTIC THIEF (Section 6, Eq. (12), p. 587). $U_i=V_i$: the thief attacks the location with the highest utility, or none if the opt-out is higher.
$$\widetilde{\mathscr P}:=\min_{x\in\mathcal X}\Big\{\max\big\{\max_{i\in N}V_i(x),\,V_0(x)\big\}\Big\}.$$
Since $V_0$ is constant, it suffices to minimize $\max_{i\in N}V_i(x)$.

BENCHMARK RULES (Section 7, Eqs. (13)-(14), p. 587): CLE and CELP with central share $\gamma\in(0,1)$ (see allocation_rules).

results.label: Observation 1
results.statement: To find an optimal budget allocation, we can also maximize the probability of no pickpocketing, because ℙ0(x) + Σ_{i∈N} ℙi(x) = 1. Formally, 𝒫 is equivalent to max_{x∈𝒳} {ℙ0(x)} = max_{x∈𝒳} 1 / (1 + Σ_{i∈N} exp{α_i − Σ_{j∈L} β_j ln(x_ij) − Σ_{k∈C} β_k ln(x_k)}) (Eq. 5). Maximizing this fraction is equivalent to minimizing its denominator, and subtracting the constant +1 does not affect an optimal solution. So 𝒫 is also equivalent to ℬ = min_{x∈𝒳} 𝔹(x), with 𝔹(x) = Σ_{i∈N} exp{α_i − Σ_{j∈L} β_j ln(x_ij) − Σ_{k∈C} β_k ln(x_k)}. For ℬ the inequality constraint of 𝒳 could be replaced by an equality, because using more budget decreases 𝔹. (Footnote 9: two problems are 'equivalent' if they have at least one optimal solution in common.)
results.meaning: The non-convex probability objective can be replaced by the total 'attraction mass' 𝔹, the sum of the exponentiated utilities, since ℙ = 𝔹/(1+𝔹) is increasing in 𝔹. Spending the whole budget is optimal.
results.proof_idea: The probabilities over N ∪ {0} sum to one. Monotone transformations of the objective keep the optimizers. 𝔹 strictly decreases in every budget component.

results.label: Lemma 1
results.statement: Let X ⊆ ℝ^n, let f, g: X → ℝ be two convex functions and α1, α2 ∈ ℝ+. Then α1·f + α2·g is a convex function on X.
results.meaning: Nonnegative combinations of convex functions are convex (a classical tool; applied repeatedly for sums of many terms).
results.proof_idea: Cited: Bazaraa, Sherali and Shetty (2013), chapter 3, page 99.

results.label: Lemma 2
results.statement: Let g: ℝ → ℝ be a non-decreasing convex function, X ⊆ ℝ^n, and h: X → ℝ a convex function. Then the composite function f: X → ℝ defined as g∘h is convex on X.
results.meaning: Composition rule, used with g = exp.
results.proof_idea: Cited: Bazaraa et al. (2013), chapter 3, page 99.

results.label: Lemma 3
results.meaning: ℙ itself is not convex (fn. 10, p. 585), but the equivalent objective 𝔹 is. A stationary point of the Lagrangian is therefore globally optimal.
results.proof_idea: Since β_j, β_k > 0, the functions −β_k ln x_k and −β_j ln x_ij are convex, and the constant α_i is convex. By Lemma 1 the exponent α_i − Σ_k β_k ln x_k − Σ_j β_j ln x_ij is convex. exp is non-decreasing and convex, so by Lemma 2 its composition is convex. Summing over i ∈ N (Lemma 1) gives convexity of 𝔹.

results.label: Theorem 1
results.statement: Suppose that 𝒢 is a convex problem on 𝒴 ⊆ ℝ^n, i.e., an optimization problem 𝒢 := min f(y) s.t. h(y) = 0, y ∈ 𝒴, with f convex on 𝒴, h linear on 𝒴, and 𝒴 an open convex set. If ȳ ∈ 𝒴 is a feasible solution of 𝒢, and ȳ together with multiplier λ ∈ ℝ satisfies ∇f(ȳ) + λ∇h(ȳ) = (0, 0, …, 0)^T, then ȳ is the global optimal solution of 𝒢 (on 𝒴).
results.meaning: Lagrange first-order conditions are sufficient for a convex objective with one linear equality over an open convex domain. It is applied to ℬ on ℝ_{++}^{|N||L|+|C|} with the binding budget (6).

results.label: Theorem 2
results.statement: The optimal budget allocation x* of ℬ, and also of 𝒫, is given by x*_k = β_k / (Σ_{m∈L} β_m + Σ_{k'∈C} β_k') · R for all k ∈ C (Eq. 7), and x*_ij = β_j / (Σ_{m∈L} β_m + Σ_{k∈C} β_k) · R · exp{α_i / (1 + Σ_{m∈L} β_m)} / Σ_{n∈N} exp{α_n / (1 + Σ_{m∈L} β_m)} for all i ∈ N and all j ∈ L (Eq. 8).
results.meaning: Two steps. First, the whole budget R is split over all resource types (central and local) in proportion to the thief's sensitivities β, so more effective resources as perceived by the thief get more. This split does not depend on the α's or on the number of locations. Second, each local resource's budget is spread over the locations with logit weights exp{α_i/(1+Σ_L β)}: MNL probabilities (over N, without opt-out) of a model whose utility is only the initial attractiveness, scaled by 1/(1+Σ_{m∈L}β_m) ('with the addition of a constant 1 for reference', p. 585). The paper's prose says 'cumulative protective impact of all resources', but the formula involves only the local β's. More attractive locations receive more local budget yet still end up with a higher pickpocket probability (Example 2: ℙ1 = 4/81 > 2/81 = ℙ2). Reader's derivation: at x*, ℙ_i(x*)/ℙ(x*) equals the weight exp{α_i/(1+Σ_Lβ)}/Σ_n exp{α_n/(1+Σ_Lβ)}, so this ordering holds in every instance.
results.proof_idea: Uses the product form of Lemma 6. The proof proposes x* and the explicit multiplier λ = −(Σ_{i∈N} exp{α_i/(1+Σ_{j∈L}β_j)})^{1+Σ_L β_j} (Σ_L β_j + Σ_C β_k)^{1+Σ_L β_j+Σ_C β_k} / (R^{1+Σ_L β_j+Σ_C β_k} Π_{k∈C} β_k^{β_k} Π_{j∈L} β_j^{β_j}). Feasibility: all components are positive and they sum to R. It then computes every partial derivative of the objective at x*, for x_ij and for x_k, and shows each equals λ, while every partial derivative of h = R − Σ x_k − ΣΣ x_ij is −1. So ∇ + λ∇h = 0, Theorem 1 gives global optimality for ℬ, and Observation 1 transfers this to 𝒫. (The appendix writes ∇ℙ and d/dx ℙ, but the expressions computed are those of 𝔹.)

results.label: Observation 2
results.statement: From Section 4, solving 𝒫̄ (Eq. 9: min_{x∈𝒳̄} ℙ(x) with 𝒳̄ = {x ∈ 𝒳 | ℙ_i(x) = ℙ_i'(x) ∀ i, i' ∈ N}) is equivalent to ℬ̄ = min_{x∈𝒳̄} 𝔹(x).
results.meaning: The fair problem can also be attacked through 𝔹. The equality constraint in 𝒳̄ is not linear, so Theorem 1 cannot be applied and a nested procedure is used instead.
results.proof_idea: Same monotone-transformation argument as Observation 1, restricted to 𝒳̄.

results.label: Lemma 4
results.statement: ℙ_i(x) = ℙ_i'(x) is equivalent to α_i − α_i' = Σ_{j∈L} β_j ln(x_ij / x_i'j) for all i, i' ∈ N.
results.meaning: The fairness condition involves only local resources. Central resources affect all locations equally and drop out. Equal probabilities are equivalent to equal deterministic utilities V_i (used in Section 6).
results.proof_idea: Write both MNL probabilities and multiply by the common positive denominator. Multiply by the positive factor exp{Σ_{k∈C} β_k ln x_k} to cancel the central terms, then take logs. (The appendix writes β_j·x_ij, β_k·x_k and a_i where β_j ln x_ij, β_k ln x_k and α_i are meant.)

results.label: Theorem 3
results.statement: The optimal fair budget allocation x̄* of 𝒫̄ reads x̄*_k = β_k / (Σ_{m∈L} β_m + Σ_{k'∈C} β_k') · R for all k ∈ C (Eq. 10), and x̄*_ij = β_j / (Σ_{m∈L} β_m + Σ_{k∈C} β_k) · R · exp{α_i / Σ_{m∈L} β_m} / Σ_{n∈N} exp{α_n / Σ_{m∈L} β_m} for all i ∈ N and all j ∈ L (Eq. 11).
results.meaning: The fairness constraint does not change the central budgets, as expected from Lemma 4, nor the split across resource types. Only the split of each local budget over locations changes. The weights become exp{α_i/Σ_L β}, 'without the reference' 1, which tilts local budget further toward more attractive locations so that all locations face the same probability. By definition ℙ(x*) ≤ ℙ(x̄*) (p. 586).
results.proof_idea: Two-part nested induction. Part 1: fix the central allocation and let R' = R − Σ_k x_k. Base case |L| = 1: the fairness condition (Lemma 4) gives x_i'1 = (exp{α_i'}/exp{α_i})^{1/β_1} x_i1; with Σ_i x_i1 = R' this gives the unique feasible split x_i1 = exp{α_i/β_1}/Σ_m exp{α_m/β_1} · R', which is Eq. (15) for |L| = 1. Induction on |L|: fix resource t+1's total R'' and apply the hypothesis to the other t local resources, with constants exp{α_i}/x_{i,t+1}^{β_{t+1}}. The remaining problem (17) is recognized as an instance of ℬ with one local resource (constant (exp{α_i})^{1/Σ_{L∖{t+1}}β}, coefficient β_{t+1}/Σ_{L∖{t+1}}β), so Theorem 2 applies. Last, the one-dimensional function D / (R''^{β_{t+1}} (R'−R'')^{Σ_{L∖{t+1}} β}) (Eq. 18) is unimodal on [0, R'] and minimized at R'' = β_{t+1}/Σ_L β · R'. Part 2: induction on |C| with the same device. Base case function D / (x_1^{β_1} (R−x_1)^{Σ_L β}) (Eq. 19), minimized at x_1 = β_1/(Σ_L β + β_1) · R. (The paper says the 'derivative is decreasing/increasing' on the two subintervals and writes the right end of the interval as 1, where R' (Part 1) and R (Part 2) are meant. What is shown is that the function decreases and then increases.)

results.label: Observation 3
results.statement: As printed: If β_j = β_k for all j ∈ L and all k ∈ C, and α_i = α_j for all i, j ∈ N, then x*_k = x̄*_k = R/(|L|·|C|) for all k ∈ C and x*_ij = x̄*_ij = R/(|L|·|C|·|N|) for all i, j ∈ N, and thus ℙ(x*) = ℙ(x̄*).
results.meaning: When the thief perceives all locations and all local and central resources as similar, the optimal allocation divides the budget equally over the resources and locations, and it is also the optimal fair allocation. NOTE: the printed denominators appear to be a typo. Substituting equal β's into Theorems 2 and 3 gives x*_k = R/(|L|+|C|) and x*_ij = R/((|L|+|C|)·|N|). The printed values are infeasible in general: with |L| = 2, |C| = 1, |N| = 2 they sum to 3R/2. (Also 'for all i, j ∈ N' should read i ∈ N, j ∈ L.)
results.proof_idea: Direct substitution into Theorems 2 and 3. With equal α's, both weight vectors are uniform.

results.label: Table 1 (comparative statics; derivations in the Appendix 'Partial derivatives of the optimal (fair) budget allocation')
results.statement: Let S = Σ_{m∈L} β_m + Σ_{k'∈C} β_k' and w_i = exp{α_i/(1+Σ_L β)} / Σ_n exp{α_n/(1+Σ_L β)}. Then: ∂x*_k/∂α_i = 0 (↔). ∂x*_k/∂β_k = R·(Σ_L β_m + Σ_{k'∈C∖{k}} β_k')/S² ≥ 0 (↗). For z ∈ L ∪ C∖{k} the paper prints ∂x*_k/∂β_z = −R·β_z/S² ≤ 0 (↘); differentiating (7) gives −R·β_k/S², so the numerator is a typo, while the sign is right. ∂x*_ij/∂α_i = R·(β_j/S)·[exp{α_i/(1+Σ_Lβ)} Σ_{n∈N∖{i}} exp{α_n/(1+Σ_Lβ)} / (1+Σ_Lβ)] / (Σ_n exp{α_n/(1+Σ_Lβ)})² ≥ 0 (↗). ∂x*_ij/∂α_i' = −R·(β_j/S)·[exp{α_i/(1+Σ_Lβ)} exp{α_i'/(1+Σ_Lβ)} / (1+Σ_Lβ)] / (Σ_n …)² ≤ 0 (↘). ∂x*_ij/∂β_k = −R·(β_j/S²)·w_i ≤ 0 (↘). ∂x*_ij/∂β_j = R·(β_j/S)·exp{α_i/(1+Σ_Lβ)}(Σ_n exp{α_n/(1+Σ_Lβ)}(α_n−α_i)/(1+Σ_Lβ)²)/(Σ_n …)² + R·(Σ_{m∈L∖{j}} β_m + Σ_C β_k)/S²·w_i (↗ or ↘). ∂x*_ij/∂β_j' = the same first term − R·(β_j/S²)·w_i (↗ or ↘). The paper states the same signs for the fair allocation x̄*, with 1/(1+Σ_L β_m) replaced by 1/Σ_L β_m everywhere.
results.meaning: A central allocation ignores location attractiveness. It grows when its own β grows and shrinks when any other resource becomes more effective. A local allocation at location i grows with α_i, shrinks when another location becomes more attractive, and shrinks when a central resource becomes more effective. It can rise or fall when its own or another local resource's β rises. Reader's reading: a larger Σ_L β flattens the location weights, which shifts budget toward less attractive locations.
results.proof_idea: Direct differentiation of the closed forms (7)-(8) and (10)-(11). (Index slip in the appendix: 'for all i ∈ N, all j ∈ N' should read j ∈ L. The ∂x*_k/∂β_z numerator should be β_k, confirmed by finite differences.)

results.label: Lemma 5
results.statement: There exists a budget allocation x ∈ 𝒳̄ that solves 𝒫̃.
results.meaning: For the deterministic thief, no loss comes from restricting to allocations where all locations have equal utility, equivalently (Lemma 4) equal pickpocket probability.
results.proof_idea: Weak-improvement argument, illustrated by Example 5. Take x ∈ 𝒳∖𝒳̄, i* ∈ argmax_i V_i(x) and j* ∈ L. Lower x_ij* at every location to x'_ij* = exp{(α_i − Σ_k β_k ln x_k − Σ_{j≠j*} β_j ln x_ij − V_i*(x))/β_j*}, so that V_i(x') = V_i*(x) for all i. Then x' ≤ x, so x' is feasible, and x' ∈ 𝒳̄ by Lemma 4. Next put the freed budget into one central resource k* (x''_k* = x'_k* + R − total of x'). This keeps utilities equal and weakly lowers all of them, so max_i V_i(x'') ≤ max_i V_i(x') = max_i V_i(x) and x'' weakly dominates x. (Small typos in the proof: a missing β_k in front of ln(x'_k), and β_j*·x'_ij* where ln is meant.)

results.label: Theorem 4
results.statement: The optimal budget allocation of 𝒫̄ solves 𝒫̃.
results.meaning: Without randomness in the thief's choice (preferences known to the policy maker), the optimal allocation equals the optimal fair allocation of Theorem 3. Reader's reading: randomness in the thief's choice is what makes unequal risks optimal. The paper adds that ignoring randomness can lead to a higher overall pickpocket probability (p. 587, shown in Section 7).
results.proof_idea: By Lemma 5 it suffices to search 𝒳̄. On 𝒳̄, Lemma 4 gives V_i(x) = V_i'(x) for all i, i', so max_i V_i = V_i for every i. Then 𝒫̃ ≡ min_{x∈𝒳̄} V_i(x) ≡ min exp{V_i(x)} ≡ |N|·min exp{V_i(x)} = min Σ_{i∈N} exp{V_i(x)} = ℬ̄, which is equivalent to 𝒫̄ by Observation 2.

results.label: Lemma 6
results.statement: For every budget allocation x ∈ 𝒳, the overall pickpocket probability equals ℙ(x) = (Σ_{i∈N} exp{α_i} / (Π_{j∈L} x_ij^{β_j} Π_{k∈C} x_k^{β_k})) / (1 + Σ_{i∈N} exp{α_i} / (Π_{j∈L} x_ij^{β_j} Π_{k∈C} x_k^{β_k})).
results.meaning: Product (Cobb-Douglas-like) form of the attraction of each location. It is the working representation in the proofs of Theorems 2 and 3.
results.proof_idea: exp{α_i − Σ_j β_j ln x_ij − Σ_k β_k ln x_k} = exp{α_i + ln(1/(Π_k x_k^{β_k} Π_j x_ij^{β_j}))} = exp(α_i)/(Π_k x_k^{β_k} Π_j x_ij^{β_j}), using b ln a = ln a^b, ln a + ln b = ln ab and exp(ln y) = y, valid because x ∈ ℝ_{++}. Then substitute into (3).

methods_and_tools: Multinomial logit (MNL) random utility model with opt-out (type-I extreme value errors), used as the thief's location choice
Log-linear (logarithmic) deterrence utility in the protective budget
Policy-maker-then-thief resource allocation with a probabilistic (quantal-response-like) offender, related by the authors to security games with quantal response
Monotone reformulation of a non-convex probability objective (min P = max P0 = min of the denominator B)
Convexity rules: nonnegative sums and composition with a non-decreasing convex function (Bazaraa, Sherali & Shetty 2013)
Sufficiency of Lagrange first-order conditions for a convex problem with one linear equality over an open convex set (Freund 2016)
Closed-form verification of stationarity with an explicit Lagrange multiplier
Nested two-step decomposition (local resources given central budget, then central) with mathematical induction on |L| and on |C|
Comparative statics by partial derivatives of closed-form solutions (Table 1)
Min-max reformulation for a deterministic attacker and a weak-domination (improvement) argument
Monte Carlo numerical experiments (1000 random instances) with box plots; benchmark heuristic rules CLE and CELP
notes.numerical_study:
SETTING (Section 7, pp. 587-590). The Paris 'pickpocket plan'. The authors lack its details and assume that policy makers use simple rules, citing Ludwig, McLean & Norton (2017) on UK police allocation practices (fn. 11). The optimal and optimal fair allocations are compared with the CLE (13) and CELP (14) rules.

INSTANCES (Section 7.1, pp. 587-588). 1000 scenarios with N = {1,2}, C = {3}, L = {4,5}:
- R: random integer between 25 and 35;
- α: chosen randomly from [0.5, 7.0];
- β (central and local): random values between [0.5, 3.5];
- γ: chosen randomly from [0.25, 0.75].
The sampling distribution is not stated; it is presumably uniform.

FIG. 3 (p. 588): deviation of the overall pickpocket probability of each allocation from that of the optimal allocation (y-axis '% Difference').
- Optimal fair: mean absolute difference 0.19%, maximum about 10.73%.
- CLE: mean 4.51%, maximum 82.22%.
- CELP: mean 3.92%, maximum 81.76%.
The paper does not define the measure. Reader's reconstruction (uniform sampling, 1000 seeded instances): in percentage points of probability the means and maxima are fair 0.18/8.1, CLE 4.35/78.3, CELP 3.60/71.2, close to the paper; relative deviations would be orders of magnitude larger, because most optimal probabilities are tiny (median 0.12%). So Fig. 3 is very likely in percentage points.

FIG. 4 (p. 589): relative percentage difference, in absolute terms, between the allocations and the optimal allocation.
- (a) Central resource: zero for the fair allocation, as Theorem 3 implies. CLE and CELP give identical box plots because they coincide on central resources (medians about 40%, boxes about 20 to 58%, whiskers up to about 110%, read from the figure).
- (b) Local resources, averaged over the four (location, local resource) pairs: smallest deviation for fair (median about 5%, outliers up to about 45%), larger for CLE (median about 55%, outliers up to about 230%), largest for CELP (median about 60%, an outlier about 450%). These numbers are approximate, read from the figure.
- Paper's reading: allocating local resources by α_i deviates more, on average, than allocating them uniformly.
- The normalization is not stated. Reader's reconstruction: dividing by the optimal allocation gives a central median of 52% and a maximum of 715%, inconsistent with panel (a); dividing by the compared allocation gives a central median of 39% (IQR 22 to 56%) and local medians of 54% (CLE) and 58% (CELP), close to the figure. Tentative.

SPECIAL EVENTS (Section 7.2, pp. 588-590). Examples: 'Le Quatorze Juillet', a World Cup final. The same 1000 instances are used, and the initial attractiveness is scaled uniformly over all locations. The paper does not state whether α_i or exp(α_i) is multiplied.

FIG. 5 (p. 589): overall probability under the optimal allocation, CLE and CELP for scale factors 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5 and 3. The fair allocation is omitted because it is close to the optimal on average (fn. 12).
- The curves are S-shaped (convex, then concave), and the transition comes earlier for CLE and CELP.
- Approximate medians read from the figure: optimal 0, 1, 7, 41, 88%; CLE 0, 5, 39, 90, 99%; CELP 0, 3, 20, 76, 97%.
- Reader's reconstruction with α_i multiplied by the scale factor: optimal 0.1, 1.0, 8.7, 49, 91%; CLE 0.5, 5.5, 41.5, 89.8, 99.1%; CELP 0.5, 3.4, 23.9, 76.7, 97.4%. Multiplying exp(α_i) instead keeps all medians below 1.5%. So the paper very likely multiplies α_i.
- Paper's claims: at a low initial probability, doubling attractiveness more than doubles the probability; at a high initial probability the increase is less than double, because the probability cannot exceed 100%.

FIG. 6 (p. 590): budget increase needed to keep the same overall probability, for scale factors 1, 1.25, 1.5, 2, 3 and 4. The allocation used is not stated; presumably the optimal one.
- The pattern is S-shaped. The y-axis is labelled '% increase in budget' but runs from 0 to 1.0.
- Approximate medians read from the figure: 0, 0.17, 0.31, 0.52, 0.78, 0.90.
- Reader's reconstruction (optimal allocation, α multiplied): medians of 1 − R/R' are 0, 0.16, 0.30, 0.51, 0.77, 0.89, matching the figure; medians of the plain increase R'/R − 1 are 0, 0.19, 0.42, 1.04, 3.34, 8.49, which do not fit the axis.
- Paper's claims: at a low initial probability, doubling attractiveness needs more than double the budget; at a high one, less than double. This insight also holds when pickpocketing decreases, e.g., in low seasons such as winter.

THREE INSIGHTS (p. 589):
1. Optimal allocation is essential, because intuitive rules may falter in specific scenarios.
2. Fairness generally performs well, with exceptions that force a choice between fairness and overall risk.
3. Keeping the probability constant during events that raise attractiveness requires more than doubling the budget when the overall probability is relatively low.
notes.worked_example:
All examples are from the paper unless marked as a reader computation. A widget can recompute everything from these formulas. With $S=\sum_{L}\beta+\sum_{C}\beta$ and $b_L=\sum_{L}\beta$:
- optimal (Theorem 2): $x^*_k=\beta_kR/S$ and $x^*_{ij}=(\beta_jR/S)\cdot\mathrm{softmax}_i(\alpha_i/(1+b_L))$;
- fair (Theorem 3): replace $1+b_L$ by $b_L$;
- evaluation: $\mathbb B=\sum_i e^{\alpha_i}/(\prod_j x_{ij}^{\beta_j}\prod_k x_k^{\beta_k})$, then $\mathbb P=\mathbb B/(1+\mathbb B)$ and $\mathbb P_i=\text{term}_i/(1+\mathbb B)$.

EXAMPLE 1 (p. 584). Paris, $N=\{1\text{ (Louvre)},2\text{ (Eiffel tower)}\}$, $C=\{3\}$ (digital campaign), $L=\{4\text{ (cameras)},5\text{ (billboards)}\}$, $R=60$, $\alpha_1=\ln16$, $\alpha_2=\ln4$, $\beta_3=1$, $\beta_4=\beta_5=0.5$.
- Allocation $x$: $x_3=24$, $x_{1,4}=6$, $x_{2,4}=12$, $x_{1,5}=6$, $x_{2,5}=12$. The terms are $16/(24\cdot6^{1/2}\cdot6^{1/2})=1/9$ and $4/(24\cdot12^{1/2}\cdot12^{1/2})=1/72$, so $\mathbb B=1/8$ and $\mathbb P(x)=(1/8)/(9/8)=1/9$.
- Allocation $x'$: $x'_3=20$, all local budgets 10. The terms are $16/200=0.08$ and $4/200=0.02$, so $\mathbb B=0.1$ and $\mathbb P(x')=1/11<1/9$. Hence $x$ is not optimal.

EXAMPLE 2 (p. 585), Theorem 2. $S=2$ and $b_L=1$.
- $x^*_3=(1/2)\cdot60=30$. Each local resource gets $(0.5/2)\cdot60=15$.
- Location weights $e^{\alpha_i/2}=4,2$, i.e., $2/3,1/3$. So $x^*_{1,4}=x^*_{1,5}=10$ and $x^*_{2,4}=x^*_{2,5}=5$.
- Terms $16/(30\cdot10)=4/75$ and $4/(30\cdot5)=2/75$, so $\mathbb B=2/25$ and $\mathbb P(x^*)=2/27\approx0.0741<1/9$.
- $\mathbb P_1(x^*)=4/81>2/81=\mathbb P_2(x^*)$: the Louvre stays riskier.

EXAMPLE 4 (p. 586), Theorem 3 on the same data. Weights $e^{\alpha_i/1}=16,4$, i.e., $0.8,0.2$.
- $\bar x^*_3=30$, $\bar x^*_{1,4}=\bar x^*_{1,5}=12$ and $\bar x^*_{2,4}=\bar x^*_{2,5}=3$.
- Each term is $16/(30\cdot12)=16/360=2/45$ and $4/(30\cdot3)=4/90=2/45$, so $\mathbb B=4/45$, $\mathbb P(\bar x^*)=4/49\approx0.0816>2/27$, and $\mathbb P_1=\mathbb P_2=2/49$.
- Reader computation: the relative cost of fairness here is $(4/49)/(2/27)-1=5/49\approx10.2\%$.

EXAMPLE 3 (p. 586). $N=\{1,2\}$, $L=\{3\}$, $C=\{4\}$, $\alpha_1=\ln4$, $\alpha_2=\ln16$, $R=5$, $\beta_3=2$, $\beta_4=1$.
- Lemma 4 gives $\ln4-\ln16=2\ln(x_{13}/x_{23})$, so $2x_{13}=x_{23}$. With $x_{13}+x_{23}=5-x_4$: $x_{13}=(5-x_4)/3$ and $x_{23}=2(5-x_4)/3$.
- Central step: $\min_{x_4\in(0,5)}\{4/(x_{13}^2x_4)+16/(x_{23}^2x_4)\}$. The paper writes this as $36/((5-x_4)^2x_4)$. Direct substitution gives $36+36=72$ in the numerator; the constant does not change the minimizer.
- Solution: $x_4=5/3$ $(=15/9)$, $\bar x_{1,3}=10/9$, $\bar x_{2,3}=20/9$. This matches Theorem 3: $x_4=\beta_4R/(\beta_3+\beta_4)$, with weights $e^{\alpha_i/2}=2,4$.

EXAMPLE 5 (p. 587), deterministic thief. $N=\{1,2\}$, $L=\{3\}$, $C=\{4\}$, $\alpha_1=4$, $\alpha_2=3$ (not logs), $R=9$, $\beta_3=3$, $\beta_4=4$.
- Start: $x_{13}=2$, $x_{23}=4$, $x_4=3$. Then $V_1=4-3\ln2-4\ln3\approx-2.47$ and $V_2=3-3\ln4-4\ln3\approx-5.55$. Location 1 is the thief's choice; location 2 has the lowest utility.
- Lower $x_{23}$ to $2e^{-1/3}\approx1.43$, so that $V_2=V_1$. Move the freed $4-2e^{-1/3}\approx2.57$ to the central resource: $x'_4=7-2e^{-1/3}\approx5.57$. The total is 9.
- Then $V_1(x')=V_2(x')\approx-4.95<\max\{V_1(x),V_2(x)\}$. (The printed sum '$x'_{1,4}+x'_{2,4}+x'_3$' is an index slip for $x'_{1,3}+x'_{2,3}+x'_4$.)
- Reader computation: Theorem 3 for these data gives $\bar x_4=36/7\approx5.14$, $\bar x_{13}\approx2.25$, $\bar x_{23}\approx1.61$, with a common $V\approx-4.98$, lower still. A direct numerical minimization of $\max\{V_1,V_2\}$ over the budget simplex gives the same point and value, consistent with Theorem 4.

READER COMPUTATIONS for the Example 1 data with $\gamma=0.5$ (not in the paper):
- CLE: $x_3=30$, every $x_{ij}=7.5$, so $\mathbb B=20/225=4/45$ and $\mathbb P=4/49$. Here it coincides with the fair optimum value.
- CELP: $x_3=30$, $x_{1j}=15\cdot\ln16/\ln64=10$, $x_{2j}=5$. This equals $x^*$, so $\mathbb P=2/27$. It is a coincidence: $\gamma=0.5=\beta_3/S$ and $\alpha_1/\alpha_2=2=e^{\alpha_1/2}/e^{\alpha_2/2}$.

CLOSED-FORM OPTIMAL VALUES (reader's derivation, implicit in the multiplier λ of the proof of Theorem 2; checked numerically on Examples 2 and 4 and on random instances):
$$\mathbb B(x^*)=Z^{1+b_L}(S/R)^S\Big/\prod_r\beta_r^{\beta_r},\quad Z=\sum_n e^{\alpha_n/(1+b_L)},$$
$$\mathbb B(\bar x^*)=|N|\,\bar Z^{\,b_L}(S/R)^S\Big/\prod_r\beta_r^{\beta_r},\quad \bar Z=\sum_n e^{\alpha_n/b_L}.$$
insights: Separation (Theorem 2): the split of R across resource types depends only on the sensitivities β (x*_k = β_k R / S). It ignores location attractiveness and the number of locations. Location attractiveness enters only in how each local budget is spread over the locations.

The abstract's 'proportional to the initial attractiveness' means proportional to exp{α_i/(1+Σ_L β)}, a softened logit transform of α. The practitioners' CELP rule is proportional to α_i itself and is a different rule.

The optimum does not equalize risk: more attractive locations get more local budget but remain riskier (Example 2: 4/81 vs 2/81). Equalizing risk requires tilting even more budget toward attractive locations (exponent α_i/Σ_L β instead of α_i/(1+Σ_L β)) and never changes the central budgets (Theorem 3, Lemma 4).

The price of fairness is small on average but not always: in Fig. 3 the mean absolute deviation in overall probability is 0.19% and the maximum about 10.73% (very likely percentage points, per a reader reconstruction). In Example 4: 4/49 vs 2/27, about 10% relative.

With a deterministic thief whose preferences are known, the min-max problem is solved by the fair allocation (Theorem 4). Reader's reading: the randomness of thief behaviour is what makes unequal risks optimal, and ignoring it pushes the planner toward the fair allocation, at a cost in overall probability; this mirrors the indifference property of Stackelberg security games with a fully rational attacker.

Convexification: ℙ is not convex, but ℙ = 𝔹/(1+𝔹) with 𝔹 = Σ_i e^{α_i} Π x^{-β} convex (Lemma 3). Lagrange stationarity on the open orthant is then sufficient (Theorem 1). Reader's note: 𝔹 is a posynomial in x, which is the structure exploited by geometric programming.
Central resources drop out of the equal-probability condition (Lemma 4). Central spending protects all locations alike, so it cannot fix inequities between locations.

Comparative statics (Table 1): central budgets ignore α. A local budget at a location rises with its own attractiveness and falls with others' attractiveness or with more effective central resources. Its response to a local resource's effectiveness is ambiguous; reader's reading: a larger Σ_L β flattens the location weights.

Reader's derivation from the first-order conditions (not stated in the paper, checked numerically): at the optimum, x*_ij = (β_j R/S) · ℙ_i(x*)/ℙ(x*), so each location's local spending is proportional to its share of the overall risk.

Simple rules (CLE, CELP) deviate from the optimal overall probability by 4.51 and 3.92 on average, with worst cases around 82 (Fig. 3, '% difference'). The paper recommends them only when locations are similar in attractiveness. Reader's caveat: even then they are optimal only if γ and the equal splits happen to match the β proportions (e.g., the Observation 3 setting with γ = |C|/(|L|+|C|)).

Special events: the overall probability grows S-shaped in a uniform scaling of attractiveness (Fig. 5). The paper claims that keeping the probability constant at a low baseline requires more than doubling the budget when attractiveness doubles (Fig. 6); a reader reconstruction does not support the link to the baseline level (see limitations).
Unlike most security games, which keep the attacker's utility linear and focus on numerical algorithms, the log-linear utility here yields closed-form results (Section 2.1).
notes.limitations_future_work:
STATED BY THE AUTHORS (Section 8, pp. 589-590):
1. Heterogeneous thieves, with varying preferences over locations and protective resources, would add realism. It may break the unimodality of the objective that is essential for the closed forms.
2. The same difficulty is expected if the goal is the expected impact (probability per location times impact) instead of the overall probability.
3. Parameter estimation is needed for real-world use: historical data on incidents and protective measures, surveys of law enforcement and security experts, and unconventional sources (social media activity, virtual environments) combined with historical records.
4. They also note that keeping the probability constant during special events may require significant additional protective resources, which matters particularly in capacity-constrained settings.

MODELLING ASSUMPTIONS VISIBLE IN THE PAPER:
- A single, homogeneous thief or group choosing one location; a static one-shot setting.
- MNL with independence of irrelevant alternatives (IIA) and an opt-out utility normalized to 0.
- A local resource's β is the same at every location.
- Every resource must receive strictly positive budget (open orthant). Reader's note: under the log utility, a zero budget would make a location infinitely attractive; the probability tends to 0 only as R goes to infinity (fn. 8).
- Continuous, divisible budget with no integer or capacity constraints.
- The thief is aware of the protection in place (p. 584); secrecy or deception (cited via Zhuang & Bier 2010, 2011) is not modelled.
- The numerical study uses only |N| = 2, |C| = 1, |L| = 2 with synthetic parameters; the sampling distributions are not stated.

UNCLEAR POINTS AND TYPOS IN THE TEXT:
- Eq. (4) numerator has β_j ln(x_j) for β_k ln(x_k).
- In Section 3.2 (p. 583), 'i ∈ 𝒞∖{∅}' should read 𝒞∖{0}.
- The Example 3 constant is 36 where substitution gives 72 (the minimizer is unaffected).
- Example 5 has an index slip in the budget sum.
- The explanation after Example 5 says budget is reduced 'for locations where the utility is not ranked lowest'. In Example 5 the budget is taken from location 2, whose utility is the lowest, and in the proof of Lemma 5 from every location whose utility is below the maximum; 'not ranked highest' is what is meant.
- Observation 3's denominators |L|·|C| look wrong; they should be |L|+|C| per Theorems 2 and 3.
- In CELP (14), the denominator Σ_{k∈L} α_k should be the sum over the locations.
- Appendix (p. 594): ∂x*_k/∂β_z is printed with numerator −β_z; the derivative of (7) is −Rβ_k/S² (same sign).
- The appendix proofs write β·x for β·ln x and a_i for α_i, and write ∇ℙ where 𝔹 is differentiated.
- In the proof of Theorem 3, 'derivative is decreasing/increasing' refers to the function, and the interval end '1' should be R' (Part 1) and R (Part 2).
- The Theorem 2 prose says 'all resources' while the formula uses only the local β's.
- Fig. 3 and Fig. 4: the type of percentage deviation and its normalization are undefined.
- Fig. 6: the scaling of attractiveness, the y-axis measure (values in [0,1] although labelled '% increase in budget') and the allocation used are not defined.

READER'S CHECK, NOT IN THE PAPER: substituting Theorem 2 gives 𝔹(x*) = Z^{1+Σ_Lβ}(S/R)^S/Πβ^β. Keeping ℙ constant when the α's change therefore needs the budget multiplier m = R'/R = (Z'/Z)^{(1+Σ_Lβ)/S}, which does not depend on R (confirmed by bisection). A simulation of the paper's instance design (uniform sampling, α multiplied by the scale factor, optimal allocation) reproduces the Fig. 6 medians if the y-axis is (R'−R)/R' = 1 − R/R'. In that reconstruction the multiplier rises with the initial probability (Spearman 0.82 at scale factor 2; median m = 1.54 in the lowest-probability quartile, where 5% of instances need more than double the budget, and m = 3.21 in the highest quartile, where 95% do). This is the reverse of the paper's verbal claim, so treat that claim as unverified; the paper's exact instance design is unknown.
notes.connections:
BUILDS ON:
(1) Resource allocation for security and prevention:
- police OR: patrol car scheduling for the NYPD by Kolesar et al. 1975 and Chaiken & Dormont 1978 (the latter's model used by over 40 US police departments, per Green & Kolesar 2004), with extensions by Green 1984, Green & Kolesar 1984, Schaack & Larson 1989, Kolesar & Green 1998; dispatching (Dunnett et al. 2019), joint dispatching and location (Adler et al. 2014); patrol sector design (D'Amico et al. 2002; Curtin et al. 2010 for Dallas; Camacho-Collados et al. 2015; Camacho-Collados & Liberatore 2015 with the Spanish National Police);
- homeland-security attacker-defender games ('stackelberg/simultaneous games'): Azaiez & Bier 2007; Bier et al. 2007, 2008; Hausken 2008; Zhuang & Bier 2007, 2010, 2011; Shan & Zhuang 2013; Guan et al. 2017; Baron, Berman & Gavious 2018; Musegaas, Schlicher & Blok 2022;
- central/general vs local/special protection: Golalikhani & Zhuang 2011; Hausken 2019 (complete characterization for two targets) and Hausken 2017 (dependent targets); layered protection by Levitin & Hausken 2012 and Levitin, Hausken & Dai 2014;
- game-theoretic security applications: airport security (Kiekintveld et al. 2009; Jain et al. 2010, used at LAX for more than 10 years), federal air marshals (Tambe et al. 2014), port container screening (Bakır 2011; Bier & Haphuriwat 2011), coast guard deployment (Shieh et al. 2012, PROTECT), wildlife rangers (Yang et al. 2014).
(2) Bounded-rational offenders through quantal response: An et al. 2013; Cheung & Bell 2021; Zhang, Wang & Zhuang 2021. Footnote 2 identifies quantal response with MNL (Jessie & Saari 2016). The paper differs by using a non-linear (log) offender utility, which allows closed-form theory.
(3) Criminology's discrete-choice approach to crime location choice: Bernasco & Nieuwbeerta 2005 (conditional logit for residential burglars' target area choice in The Hague); Curtis-Ham et al. 2021; Ruiter 2017; Weisburd et al. 2009; Kuralarasan & Bernasco 2022; Frith 2019; Villegas et al. 2022.
(4) Choice-based optimization (CBO): Paneque et al. 2021, 2022; Roemer, Müller & Voigt 2022; revenue management assortment and pricing under various choice models (Rusmevichientong et al. 2014, MNL with random parameters; Nip et al. 2021, single transition model; Dong et al. 2019, Markov chain model; Li et al. 2022, linear nested stochastic model); choice-based facility location (school, health care, retail, park-and-ride), traffic assignment, routing and supply chain contracting. The paper claims a new CBO problem and domain: resource allocation for security and prevention.

AUTHORS' OWN WORK CITED:
- Musegaas, Schlicher & Blok (2022), 'Stackelberg production-protection games: Defending crop production against intentional attacks', EJOR 297(1), 102-119.
- Bierlaire & Lurkin (2017), 'Introduction to disaggregate demand models', in Leading developments from INFORMS communities, pp. 48-67.

READER'S NOTE ON THIS STUDY SET: of the other papers in the set, it cites only the production-protection paper. It shares the defender-attacker protection theme with the production-protection, time-dependent Stackelberg protection location and rapid-response-team papers (all Stackelberg/leader-follower) and with the bodyguard paper (a simultaneous two-person zero-sum game, not Stackelberg), which acknowledges the same NWO grant VI.Veni.201E.017. It shares MNL choice modelling with the choice-based collaborative price-setting paper. It contains no cooperative-game content.
prerequisites: Discrete choice and random utility theory: MNL probabilities, Gumbel/type-I extreme value errors, alternative-specific constants, opt-out alternatives, IIA
Convex analysis: convex functions, sums and compositions, log and exp properties
Lagrange multipliers and the sufficiency of first-order conditions for convex problems with linear equality constraints
Monotone transformations of objectives and the notion of equivalent problems
Mathematical induction for nested optimization arguments
One-dimensional optimization of functions like y^{-a}(R−y)^{-b} (Cobb-Douglas-type optimality: shares proportional to exponents)
Stackelberg security games and quantal response equilibrium basics
Reading box plots in Monte Carlo experiments

glossary.definition: Decision maker (e.g., a city mayor) who allocates the budget R over protective resources and locations to minimize the overall pickpocket probability.
Someone who has plans to pickpocket (fn. 1); may be a single person or an organized group of homogeneous individuals planning to pickpocket one location (fn. 3).
Candidate target, e.g., the Eiffel tower, the Louvre, the Sacré-Coeur, Montmartre.
Resource that protects one specific location, e.g., security cameras, billboards or police officers at a metro station. Budget x_ij per location i and type j.
Resource that protects all locations at once, e.g., a social-media awareness campaign or the Boefproof app. Budget x_k.
Vector x = ((x_ij)_{i∈N, j∈L}, (x_k)_{k∈C}) in the open positive orthant with total spending at most R.
The thief's choice not to pickpocket any location in N (another city or district, or staying home); its utility is normalized to 0.
Initial interest or attractiveness of location i (tourist numbers, distance to the thief's home, escape possibilities).
Thief's sensitivity to the risk perceived from a protective resource type; utility falls by β ln(budget).
Sum over locations of the MNL probabilities ℙ_i(x), i.e., 1 − ℙ0(x).
Sum over locations of exp(V_i(x)) = e^{α_i}/(Π_j x_ij^{β_j} Π_k x_k^{β_k}); minimizing it is equivalent to minimizing ℙ, since ℙ = 𝔹/(1+𝔹).
Problems that have at least one optimal solution in common (fn. 9).
Optimal allocation under the constraint that every location faces the same pickpocket probability (set 𝒳̄).
Variant without random error, U_i = V_i: the thief picks the highest-utility location, or opts out; the problem becomes min-max utility (𝒫̃).
Random utility model with i.i.d. EV(0,1) errors giving choice probabilities e^{V_i}/Σ_j e^{V_j}.
Bounded-rationality model in security games in which offenders observe rewards with error and respond probabilistically; its expressions coincide with the MNL (fn. 2).
Optimization problems that embed a discrete choice model of other actors' behaviour (revenue management, facility location, routing, now security).
Central and Location-Equal: a share γ of R split equally over central resources, the rest equally over local resources and locations (Eq. 13).
Central-Equal and Location-Proportional: like CLE, but the local budget is split proportionally to α_i (Eq. 14).
Uniform multiplier of the initial attractiveness of all locations, used to mimic special events such as 14 July or a World Cup final (a reader reconstruction indicates it multiplies α_i).

Dutch national awareness campaign that encourages citizens to activate or install an anti-theft feature on mobile devices so they can be made non-accessible remotely; part of a larger Ministry of Security and Justice campaign.
European collaborative initiative led by Belgium with Europol, with the Netherlands and the UK as partners, aiming at a European policy cycle against organized and serious transnational crime.

study_questions: Why is ℙ(x) not convex while 𝔹(x) is, and why do 𝒫 and ℬ have the same optimal solutions (Observation 1, fn. 9)? Why does the budget bind?
Write the Lagrange conditions for ℬ and derive x*_k = β_k R/S. Why does the central budget not depend on any α_i?
Show that, at a stationary point, x*_ij is proportional to β_j times the location's share of the risk, and use this to recover the weights exp{α_i/(1+Σ_L β)}. Where does the '1' come from?
Prove Lemma 4. Why do central resources disappear from the fairness condition, and what does that imply for Theorem 3's central budgets?
Recompute Examples 1, 2 and 4: allocations, ℙ, ℙ_1 and ℙ_2. What is the relative cost of fairness in this instance?
In Example 3, carry out the substitution yourself. Is the constant 36 or 72, and does it matter?
Explain the weak-improvement construction of Lemma 5 using Example 5. Which location loses budget, and why does Theorem 4 imply that a planner who ignores randomness ends up with the fair allocation?
Check Observation 3 against Theorem 2 for |L| = 2, |C| = 1, |N| = 2. Is the printed allocation feasible, and what is the correct expression?
Interpret each sign in Table 1. Differentiate (7) yourself: is the numerator of ∂x*_k/∂β_z equal to β_z or β_k? Why can x*_ij rise or fall when β_j increases?

Compare CLE and CELP with the optimum. Under which parameter patterns do they coincide with it (e.g., the Observation 3 setting with γ = |C|/(|L|+|C|) for CLE, or the Example 1 data with γ = 0.5 for CELP)?
How does this model relate to Stackelberg security games with quantal-response attackers? Who moves first, who responds, and what does the log-linear utility buy analytically?
What would change with heterogeneous thieves (mixed or latent-class logit), or with an expected-impact objective, and why would the closed forms break?

Using the closed form 𝔹(x*) = Z^{1+Σ_Lβ}(S/R)^S/Πβ^β, how much budget is needed to keep ℙ constant when all α_i double? Does the answer depend on R? Does it support the paper's claim about low versus high initial probabilities?
How could α and β be estimated from incident data or expert surveys, as the authors propose?

changes: Worked example, Example 4 (p. 586): the second term was written '4/120'; it is 4/(30*3) = 4/90 = 2/45. Corrected.

Quantified the claim that the multiplier rises with the initial probability (Spearman 0.82; quartile medians 1.54 vs 3.21; 5% vs 95% of instances need more than double the budget).

Motivation (p. 581): Fig. 1 shows billboards and a sprayed template, not every campaign listed. The Paris plan was revealed by a June 2022 news bulletin (Bijlsma, 2022); the paper does not date the reactivation. Added the 40 million visitors in 2018 (Gadaud, 2019) and attributed the EUR 218-282 billion estimate to the SOCTA report as cited.
Bibliography (p. 590): the ChatGPT statement says 'select content and sentences', not 'select sentences'. Added the license URL.
Model: 'Stackelberg-like' is now marked as the reader's characterization. The paper never calls its own model Stackelberg; it relates it to security games with quantal response (Section 2.1, fn. 2).

Connections (p. 583): the revenue-management references are not all 'under MNL'. Rusmevichientong et al. 2014 uses MNL with random parameters, Nip et al. 2021 a single transition model, Dong et al. 2019 a Markov chain model and Li et al. 2022 a linear nested stochastic model. Also renamed 'deployed Stackelberg security games' to the paper's 'game-theoretic security applications' and added the police-OR extensions the paper cites.

Reader's note on the study set: the bodyguard paper is a simultaneous two-person zero-sum game, not Stackelberg (it shares NWO grant VI.Veni.201E.017). Of the other papers in the set, only the production-protection paper (Musegaas, Schlicher & Blok 2022) is cited.

Limitations (p. 587): the 'not ranked lowest' wording after Example 5 is now stated as reversed. In Example 5 the budget is cut at location 2, which has the lowest utility, so 'not ranked highest' is meant.

Insights, allocation rules and study questions: CLE and CELP are not optimal just because locations are similar (Observation 3). They also need gamma = Sum_C beta/S, equal betas within C and within L, and matching location weights. CELP coincides with x* on the Example 1 data because gamma = 0.5 = beta_3/S.

Theorem 2 and allocation rules: replaced the general claim that the optimum is 'generally not fair' with the paper's Example 2 plus a marked reader derivation. P_i(x*)/P(x*) equals the logit weight, so the more attractive location is always riskier (checked numerically).
Theorem 4 meaning and Table 1 meaning: interpretive sentences (randomness makes unequal risks optimal; a larger Sum_L beta flattens the weights) are now marked as the reader's reading.
Glossary: Boefproof and the quantal-response definitions now follow the paper's wording more closely. The scale-factor entry notes that a reader reconstruction indicates alpha_i is multiplied.
